title: Nearly 70% of Diet and Exercise Videos Are Misleading
paragraphs: Social media is full of content creators telling us what to eat and how to exercise to get the "perfect" body.

And while there's nothing wrong with wanting to eat well and get in shape, having a very strict program of diet and exercise can be problematic if it becomes obsessive — and especially if it isn't based on accurate information.
In fact, a new study has found that nearly 70% of diet and exercise advice on platforms like TikTok and Instagram is misleading.
Researchers from Australia looked at 300 TikTok and Instagram videos with health or diet hashtags, including "healthy lifestyle," "clean eating" and "nutrition."
For each hashtag, the researchers looked at the first 50 videos on both TikTok and Instagram.
The researchers checked all 300 videos for things like lists of "good" and "bad" foods, or strict eating habits and exercise plans. They also checked the accuracy of the information in the videos.
The researchers then looked for each content creator on Google and LinkedIn to see if they had any qualifications related to the content in their videos.
The results showed that 68% of the nutrition and exercise information in the videos was misleading or false. And about 6% of videos had information that could be harmful.
The biggest problem was that many content creators were not qualified.
Unqualified creators made up 78% of those studied, while only 22% had recognized qualifications in health or nutrition.
Qualified creators were much more likely to share accurate information — 46% of their videos were accurate. But just 5% of videos from unqualified creators were accurate.
So while we might want to eat right and get in shape so we can look like our favorite content creators, in most cases, listening to them about how to do it isn't the best idea.
